docs.title: About
docs.text: This package implements a Bayesian Impulse-Response Model for athletic performance. The default prior structure is physiologically informed and resolves inference issues common in the literature, and the model allows for multivariate inputs and outputs so that parameters can be informed by multiple metrics of performance.

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
Suppose you want to estimate the impacts of daily training load on running speed performance. You have temperature measurements for each outdoor run and an indicator for each indoor treadmill run, and you want the model to control for potential affects these exogenous variables have on running speed. You also have daily-ish heart rate variability data, which you have noticed correlates with running speed, and which you notice is commonly suppressed the day after intense training.

Suppose you track loads and metrics in different tables. Each sheet has a date column, a value column named after the metric, and the exogenous variables. Blank cells mark unobserved days. You prepare your data into a Panel:

import pandas as pd

# has columns 'w' (training load) and 'date' (YYYY-MM-DD)
training_load_df = pd.read_csv("/path/to/training_load.csv")

# has columns 'hrv', 'w' (missing on rest days) and 'date'
hrv_df = pd.read_csv("/path/to/hrv.csv")

# has columns 'speed', 'temp', 'indoor' (1 or 0) and 'date'
speed_df = pd.read_csv("/path/to/speed.csv")

sheets = {"w": training_load_df, "hrv": hrv_df, "speed": speed_df}

panel = Panel.from_sheets(
    sheets,
    date="date",
    load="w",
    exog={"hrv": ["w"], "speed": ["temp", "indoor"]},
).standardize()

To fit the model in which the classical Banister parameters are jointly estimated from both HRV and speed controlling for their corresponding exogenous variables:

model = IRModel(
    load=Load("w"),  # the training-load driver
    fitness="banister",
    fatigue="banister",
    metrics=(
        Metric("hrv", exog=("w",)),  # hrv suppression
        Metric("speed", exog=("temp", "indoor")),  # heat + treadmill effects
    ),
)
idata = model.fit(panel, sampler=dict(draws=1000, tune=2000, seed=0))

idata is an ArviZ InferenceData. Summarize the fit and extract the shared stock R_t:

import arviz as az

az.summary(idata, var_names=["k_F", "k_G", "tau_F", "tau_G"], ci_prob=0.95)  # mean, 95% CI, r_hat
R_mean = idata.posterior["R"].mean(("chain", "draw"))  # posterior-mean R_t trajectory
idata.to_netcdf("fit.nc")  # cache for later reuse

docs.title: standardize()
docs.text:
Center/scale each response and its exog, rescale load to average-day units.

Each response metric's values and exog columns are z-scored (center/scale stored in scaling for back-transform); load is rescaled by its own mean so gains stay \(O(1)\).

docs.title: birm.model
docs.text: The impulse-response model specification.

docs.title: IRModel dataclass
docs.text:
Declarative spec of the shared-stock multivariate impulse-response model.

Selects one impulse-response core \(R_t\) via fitness \(\times\) fatigue and attaches one observation layer per Metric. Call fit with a Panel to sample.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default load Load

The training-load driver \(w_t\).

required fitness str

Fitness core \(M_F\); one of banister, ceddia_periodize, ceddia_taper, ceddia.

required fatigue str

Fatigue core; one of banister, busso, none.

required metrics tuple[Metric, ...]

Response metrics sharing the single latent stock.

required priors dict[str, Prior]

Optional overrides for named model parameters (e.g. k_p, k_a, tau_v).

dict() parameterization str

Latent-stock prior geometry; one of informed, admissible, or direct. informed (default) samples the identifiable reparameterized margins (\(\theta, \lambda_F, \lambda_G\)) so the gain ratio and timescale ordering \(\tau_v < \tau_G < \tau_F\) and \(k_G > k_F\) hold with certainty (off the \(\tau_F = \tau_G\) ridge). admissible is identical but floors the gain ratio at the Ceddia (2026) admissibility metric \(a_c\) via \(k_G = (a_c + \theta) k_F\), so \(P(k_G/k_F > a_c) = 1\) in the posterior. direct instead samples \(k_F\), \(k_G\), \(\tau_F\), \(\tau_G\) (and Busso \(\tau_v\)) independently from weakly-informative HalfNormal/LogNormal priors over wide ranges, with no ordering or gain-ratio constraint -- the ill-conditioned baseline the reparameterization is designed to fix.

'informed'

docs.title: Building a Panel
docs.text: The Panel is the model-ready dataset used by birm. It holds one contiguous daily grid along with the observed values and their positions on that grid. Training load is required on every day and is therefore imputed where missing (a missing day is a rest day, 0.0 load). Each metric and its corresponding exogenous variables keeps its own observation cadence; days can be missing per metric independently.

docs.title: Long form
docs.text:
Use this if you have one long table containing all your measurements. Each row is a (date, metric, value) reading.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from birm import Panel

# create example data as a long-form pandas dataframe
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "date": ["2025-01-03", "2025-01-03", "2025-01-04", "2025-01-06"],
        "metric": ["w", "hrv", "hrv", "speed"],
        "value": [210.0, 64.0, 61.0, 4.71],
        "trimp": [np.nan, 210.0, 185.0, np.nan],  # HRV-day exog
        "temp": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, 27.5],  # speed-day exog
        "indoor": [np.nan, np.nan, np.nan, 1.0],
    }
)

panel = Panel.from_long(
    df,
    date="date",
    metric="metric",
    value="value",
    load="w",  # which label is the training load
    exog={"hrv": ["trimp"], "speed": ["temp", "indoor"]},
)

panel.T  # 4 — days from 2025-01-03 to 2025-01-06
panel.metrics["hrv"].idx  # array([0, 1]) — grid positions of the two HRV readings
panel.metrics["speed"].exog  # {"temp": array([27.5]), "indoor": array([1.0])}
panel.densest()  # "hrv" has the most observations

docs.title: Wide / multi-sheet
docs.text:
Use this if you track loads and metrics in different tables. Each sheet has a date column, a value column named after the metric, and (possibly) exogenous variables. Blank cells mark unobserved days.

# create an example dataset as a dict of multiple wide-form dataframes
sheets = {
    "w": pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2025-01-03"], "w": [210.0]}),
    "hrv": pd.DataFrame(
        {"date": ["2025-01-03", "2025-01-04"], "hrv": [64.0, 61.0], "trimp": [210.0, 185.0]}
    ),
    "speed": pd.DataFrame(
        {"date": ["2025-01-06"], "speed": [4.71], "temp": [27.5], "indoor": [1.0]}
    ),
}

panel = Panel.from_sheets(
    sheets, date="date", load="w", exog={"hrv": ["trimp"], "speed": ["temp", "indoor"]}
)

docs.title: Standardizing
docs.text:
standardize() z-scores each metric and its exog (storing (center, scale) in panel.scaling for back-transform) and rescales load to average-day units so the model's gains stay O(1):

panel = panel.standardize()
panel.scaling["hrv"]  # (center, scale) used to un-standardize HRV forecasts later

The stored scaling is what forecast and simulation reuse to put future load on the model's scale and to back-transform predictions.

docs.title: Specifying a model
docs.text:
Once you have a Panel, an IRModel declares which impulse-response model to fit. The IR model is composed of antagonistic terms R_t = f_t - g_t, with f_t and g_t commonly called fitness and fatigue. You choose which form each term can take.

The IR model is shared across metrics, and each metric gets its own exogenous predictors and, optionally, an AR1 term orthogonalized against the intercept and the gain-free fitness and fatigue integrals so that it only explains variability not already explained by the drivers of primary importance.

from birm import IRModel, Load, Metric

model = IRModel(
    load=Load("w"),  # the training-load driver w_t
    fitness="banister",
    fatigue="banister",  # the R_t core
    metrics=(
        Metric("hrv", exog=("w",), ar1=True),  # beta^(hrv) suppression + u^(hrv) drift
        Metric("speed", exog=("temp", "indoor")),  # heat + treadmill adjustments; sparse, no u
    ),
)

docs.title: Choosing the core
docs.text:
fitness × fatigue select the shared R_t. Setting the Ceddia gains k_p = k_a = 0 recovers the Banister linear model.

Argument Options Meaning fitness banister original linear fitness gain ceddia_periodize periodization via fatigue feedback (k_p) ceddia_taper tapering via diminishing dose returns (k_a) ceddia both (k_p and k_a) fatigue banister original linear fatigue busso variable-dose, time-varying k_G(s) (tau_v) none fitness-only model

docs.title: Describing each metric
docs.text:
Each Metric is a noisy, optionally transformed readout of the shared stock. Every term but the impulse response and white noise is optional; drop one by leaving it off.

Metric(
    "speed",
    link="identity",  # l^(j): "identity" | "log" | "logit"
    exog=("temp", "indoor"),  # X^(j) columns -> beta^(j)
    ar1=True,  # include the orthogonalized slow-drift term u^(j)
    intercept=True,  # include the baseline alpha^(j)
    gamma=None,  # fix the scale; None -> densest metric auto-pinned to gamma == 1
)
  • link applies a nonlinear transform between the latent stock and the measurement.
  • exog names columns that this metric carries in the panel (panel.metrics[name].exog); a reference to a missing column is an error at fit time.
  • ar1 adds the lag-1 process u^(j), orthogonalized against the intercept and the gain-free fitness and fatigue integrals to capture slow unexplained drift — use it for densely observed metrics; omit it for sparse ones.
  • intercept adds the baseline alpha^(j); drop it only when the baseline is already removed (e.g. a differenced metric) or owned by another term.
  • gamma pins the per-metric scale. Leave it None and the densest metric is auto-pinned to gamma == 1, tying the latent scale to the best-observed channel.

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text:
.fit() fits the model by drawing posterior samples of the parameters:

idata = model.fit(panel, sampler=dict(draws=1000, tune=2000, seed=0))

idata is an ArviZ InferenceData holding the posterior draws. Inspect parameters, check convergence, and recover the latent impulse-response stock R_t:

import arviz as az

az.summary(idata, var_names=["k_F", "k_G", "tau_F", "tau_G"], ci_prob=0.95)  # mean, 95% CI, r_hat
az.plot_trace(idata, var_names=["k_F", "tau_F"])  # convergence diagnostics

R = idata.posterior["R"]  # (chain, draw, T) latent stock
lo, mid, hi = R.quantile([0.025, 0.5, 0.975], dim=("chain", "draw"))  # 95% credible band
idata.to_netcdf("fit.nc")  # cache for later reuse

docs.title: Overriding priors
docs.text:
Pass Prior objects keyed by parameter name to override defaults (e.g. the Ceddia k_p/k_a or Busso tau_v):

from birm import Prior

model = IRModel(
    load=Load("w"),
    fitness="ceddia_periodize",
    fatigue="banister",
    metrics=(Metric("hrv"),),
    priors={"k_p": Prior("HalfNormal", {"sigma": 0.5})},
)

docs.title: Model Description
docs.text: The purpose of this package is to unify multiple variants of the impulse-response model under a single, modular, Bayesian framework, and to resolve some of its statistical flaws by sharing information across different metrics and by mitigating ill-conditioned parameter spaces with physiologically meaningful restricted priors.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The Banister impulse-response model (and its many variants) provides insights into the effects of training on performance through the inference of athetic performance's responses to training dose as well as the prediction of future performance. It suffers from two interacting challenges: performance data are expensive and physically demanding to collect and therefore sparsely observed, and the parameters of interest are ill-conditioned. Without a dense, high-signal dataset from which to learn, actionable insights from posterior parameter estimates and performance forecasts are unlikely.

docs.title: The original model
docs.text:
The original Banister 1975, Calvert 1976 model is defined by

\[p_t = p_0 + k_F\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_F} - k_G\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_G}\]

where \(p_0\) is an initial performance value and \(p_t\) and \(w_t\) are performance and training load at time \(t\), respectively. The first and second summands above are commonly called "fitness" and "fatigue" and are described by their gain parameters \(k_F, k_G\) and decay rates \(\tau_F, \tau_G\).

docs.title: Statistical flaws in the original model
docs.text:
Hellard 2006 first quantified the ill-conditioning issue. Using nine elite swimmers with an average of 13 performances across a single training season, it was demonstrated that, even though goodness-of-fit was strong (average \(R^2 \approx 0.79\)), the uncertainty in the parameter estimates was wide (the bootstrapped coefficient of variation was over 30% for the decay parameters and 60% for the gain parameters). This ill-conditioning was primarily caused by correlation of the posterior estimates (0.91 for the gain terms and 0.99 for the decay rates). In other words, there is a large set of widely varying parameter combinations that give similar model errors. It isn't difficult to see why: fitness and fatigue are antagonistic terms competing to explain changes in sparsely observed performance using similar time-filters on the same training load variable.

Vermeire 2022 reproduced Hellard's result with eight performance observations on a cycle ergometer from a single subject and visualized the model error over a grid of parameter combinations, further demonstrating that (a) the error landscape over \(\tau_F\) and \(\tau_G\) is characterized by a sharp ridge near \(\tau_F = \tau_G\), and (b) the physiologically sensible region in which incremental fitness gains are smaller than fatigue gains, \(k_F < k_G\), results in consistently lower error than the unreasonable alternative.

Peng 2024 built the first Bayesian Banister model. Importantly, they use informative prior parameterizations to provide a prior belief about values the parameters can take based on existing results from the literature. Importantly, they impose an informative prior structure by reparameterizing \(k_G = \theta k_F\) and imposing the constraint \(\theta > 1\); in other words, preventing the model from considering the physiologically unreasonable region \(k_F > k_G\) that Vermeire demonstrated resulted in poor model fit. They demonstrate that the Bayesian approach resulted in better parameter estimates, though uncertainty was still large, likely due to fitting the model to only 13 performance measurements (with additional noise likely caused by each performance being races of different lengths, and by imputing some missing training loads).

Marchal 2025 also take a Bayesian approach and test weakly- versus moderately-informed Bayesian priors. However, they drop the physiological constraint \(\theta > 1\) and use performance measurements from short-track speed skaters previously demonstrated to be low-signal (average \(R^2 \approx 0.20\)) via alternative machine learning methods. Furthermore, their MCMC traceplots demonstrate a single stuck chain, which may be indicative of a poorly tuned sampler rather than model issues. They conclude that the impulse response model presents major dysfunctions, though their conclusion rests on an estimate of a posterior distribution that did not converge, and on cross-validation applied to a small set of performance measurements (roughly 35 performances from nine athletes, of which roughly ten performances are allocated to the testing dataset).

docs.title: The BIRM Prior
docs.text:
The ill-conditioning issue is mitigated with a reparameterization. BIRM adopts Peng's constraint \(k_F < k_G\) to restrict the model to only search for optimal parameter combinations in a physiologically reasonable space. To motivate similar reparameterizations for the decay terms, we represent \(k_G/k_F\) in terms of decay rates and the time it takes the impulse response to recover \(t_r\) and peak \(t_p\):

\[k_G/k_F = (\tau_F/\tau_G)^{\left(\frac{1}{t_p/t_r - 1}\right)} \]

This satisfies the constraint \(k_G/k_F > 1\) either when \(\tau_F > \tau_G\) and \(t_p > t_r\), or when \(\tau_F < \tau_G\) and \(t_p < t_r\). The former is the physiologically reasonable scenario: fitness is accumulated over longer timescales than fatigue, and the impulse response recovers before it peaks.

In Ceddia 2026, the authors derive an admissibility condition implied by bounded infinite-horizon optimal training policies (i.e., finite human performance):

\[ k_G \left(1 + \frac{1}{e^{1/\tau_G} - 1}\right) - \frac{k_F}{e^{1/\tau_F} - 1} > 0 \]

Rearranging to express the condition in terms of our earlier reparameterization, we see that

\[k_G/k_F > \frac{1 - e^{-1/\tau_G}}{ e^{1/\tau_F} - 1} \equiv a_c\]

It can be shown via Taylor expansion that

\[\frac{1}{\log(2 - e^{-1/\tau_G})} = \tau_G + 1 + \mathcal{O}(1/\tau_G^2)\]

and therefore admissibility \(a_c\) approximately satisfies the condition \(a_c > 1\) when \(\tau_F > \tau_G + 1\). BIRM therefore provides the following two parameterizations: the informed version is

\[k_G = (\phi + 1) k_F \quad \text{ and } \quad \tau_F = 1 + \tau_G + \lambda_F,\] \[\phi \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\phi, \sigma_\phi^2),\] \[\lambda_F \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_{\lambda_F}, \sigma_{\lambda_F}^2)\]

which produce posterior estimates which satisfy the constraints \(k_G/k_F > 1\) and \(\tau_F > \tau_G + 1\) with certainty. Note that \(k_G/k_F > 1\) and the (approximately) implied \(a_c > 1\) is weaker than the admissibility condition \(k_G/k_F > a_c\). The admissible version imposes the stronger constraint such that posterior admissibility is certain:

\[k_G = (\phi + a_c) k_F \quad \text{ and } \quad \tau_F = 1 + \tau_G + \lambda_F,\] \[\phi \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\phi, \sigma_\phi^2),\] \[\lambda_F \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_{\lambda_F}, \sigma_{\lambda_F}^2)\]

Note that strictly imposing \(k_G/k_F > a_c\) can bias parameter estimates from athletes who have not yet reached peak performance.

docs.title: Multivariate Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Assimilating additional data alongside performance (e.g., heart rate variability from consumer wearables) and controlling for performance effect modifiers (e.g., temperature and other external stressors) can further refine parameter estimates and improve forecast performance. To set notation, let \(w_t\) be training load, \(f_t\) be fitness, \(g_t\) be fatigue, and \(R_t = f_t - g_t\) be the impulse response on day \(t\). Multiple target variables (e.g., HRV and speed) can be represented as transformed, noisy measurements of the underlying IR model. The \(j^{th}\) response variable \(j=1,...,J\) at time \(t\), \(Y^{(j)}_t\), is given by

\[ Y^{(j)}_t = \alpha^{(j)} + \gamma^{(j)} l^{(j)}\left(R_t\right) + X^{(j)}_t\beta^{(j)} + u^{(j)}_t + \epsilon^{(j)}_t\]

where \(\alpha^{(j)}\) is the intercept analogous to initial performance \(p_0\) in Banister's formulation, \(\gamma^{(j)}\) is a regression parameter for the linear relationship between the measurement and the transformed latent impulse response model, \(l^{(j)}(\cdot)\) is a link function to represent nonlinear relationships across measurement types, and \(\beta^{(j)}\) are coefficients corresponding to exogenous predictors \(X^{(j)}\).

Residuals are composed into two terms: \(\epsilon^{(j)}_t \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\epsilon)\) representing IID noise, and \(u^{(j)}_t\), a lag-1 autoregressive process orthogonalized to lie in the null space of the intercept and the fitness and fatigue integrals and capturing variation (e.g., slow drift due to unmeasured stress and fatigue, daily responses to sleep and nutrition, etc.) not explained by the main effects.

In this package, every term except the impulse-response \(R_t\) and the white noise \(\epsilon^{(j)}_t\) is optional. Note that there are \(J+1\) possible time grids; they are "ragged" in that training loads \(w_t\) and channels \(Y^{(j)}_t\) exist on their own measurement cadence. Each day may or may not have an observation from each channel, independently.

docs.title: Modifications to the impulse-response model
docs.text:
The original Banister 1975 IR model is defined by

\[R^{(O)}_t = k_F\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_F} - k_G\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_G}\]

Busso 2003 modified the fatigue gain to vary over time by responding to training load:

\[R^{(V)}_t = k_F\sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_F} - \sum_{s=0}^{t-1}k_G(s) w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_G},\] \[k_G(t) = \sum_{s=0}^{t-1} w_s e^{-(t-s)/\tau_v}.\]

The nonlinear fatigue gain accumulates with more recent training on timescales that are expected to be smaller than fitness and fatigue level. We therefore impose the physiological constraint \(\tau_F > \tau_G > \tau_v\) with the reparameterization \(\tau_G = \tau_v + \lambda_G\) and \(\tau_F = 1 + \tau_G + \lambda_F\) with log-normal priors on \(\lambda_G\) and \(\lambda_F\).

Ceddia 2026 studied the optimal training routines implied by Banister and Busso's models and devised their own modifications that induce periodization and tapering:

\[R^{(C)}_t = \sum_{s=0}^{t-1}M_F(w_s, g_s)e^{-(t-s)/\tau_F} - k_G\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}w_s\,e^{-(t-s)/\tau_G}\]

All nonlinearity lives in the fitness-gain function \(M_F(w_s, g_s)\); Ceddia's Eq. (17) leaves the fatigue impulse linear in \(w_s\) (he explicitly declines to modify the fatigue response, as that "would amount to redefining the training impulse itself"). Setting \(k_p = k_a = 0\) recovers \(M_F = k_F w_s\), the Banister linear model.

Periodization is induced by fatigue feedback: diminishing gain as fatigue accumulates (cf. Ceddia Eq. (28))

\[M_F(w_s, g_s) = \frac{k_F w_s}{1 + k_p g_s}, \]

and tapering is induced by diminishing returns in the impulse (cf. Ceddia Eqs. (19)–(21))

\[M_F(w_s, g_s) = \frac{k_F w_s}{1+k_a w_s}\]

and both by

\[M_F(w_s, g_s) = \frac{k_F w_s}{(1 + k_p g_s)(1+k_a w_s)}.\]

docs.title: Example: HRV and speed
docs.text:
\(Y^{(1)}_t\) and \(Y^{(2)}_t\) are HRV and speed, respectively. \(X^{(1)}_t\) is the training load \(w_t\) to represent a possible daily HRV suppression effect \(\beta^{(1)}_t\), and \(X^{(2)}_t\) contains outdoor temperature (to adjust for heat) and an indicator of whether each run was performed indoors on a treadmill, giving speed two exogenous predictors. HRV is observed near daily, so we include a \(u^{(1)}_t\) term. speed is more sparsely observed; no \(u\) is warranted. Both channels use the identity link \(l^{(1)}(x) = l^{(2)}(x) = x\), and we set \(\gamma^{(1)} \equiv 1\) so the scale of the IR model is pinned to the more densely observed channel HRV. The shared impulse-response model is the Ceddia variant whose optimal training sequence is characterized by periodization and tapering. The joint model is therefore

\[ Y^{(1)}_t = \alpha^{(1)} + R^{(C)}_t + X^{(1)}_t\beta^{(1)} + u^{(1)}_t + \epsilon^{(1)}_t\] \[ Y^{(2)}_t = \alpha^{(2)} + \gamma^{(2)} R^{(C)}_t + X^{(2)}_t\beta^{(2)} + \epsilon^{(2)}_t\]

You would define this model in BIRM like so:

model = IRModel(
    load=Load("w"),  # the training-load driver w_t
    fitness="ceddia",
    fatigue="banister",
    metrics=(
        Metric("hrv", exog=("w",), ar1=True),  # hrv suppression + drift (u)
        Metric("speed", exog=("temp", "indoor")),  # heat + treadmill effects
    ),
)
